title: Renting your wardrobe
context: You will hear an interview with Jess Morgan, who started a clothing-rental business while she was at university.

unit.style: a natural radio interview, lively and articulate, at a normal pace

turns.text: My guest today is Jess Morgan, who started a clothing-rental business while she was still at university. Jess, where did the idea come from?

Honestly, from my own wardrobe. I had a cupboard full of clothes I'd worn once, for a wedding or a party, and then never again. I worked out that I'd spent more on those than on my rent one year, which was a bit of a shock. And when I asked my friends, they all had the same problem. So the idea wasn't really clever. It was just obvious once you looked.
Lots of people have obvious ideas. What made you actually do it?

A business competition at my university. There was a prize of five thousand pounds, and I entered mainly because a friend dared me to. I didn't win, as it happens. I came third. But one of the judges ran a logistics company, and she offered to give me advice. That turned out to be worth far more than the prize money.

Because that's the hard part of renting clothes, and I hadn't realised. Everyone imagines the challenge is finding customers. It isn't. The challenge is getting a dress cleaned, checked and back to the next person in forty-eight hours without losing it. In our first year, we lost more money on delivery mistakes than on anything else.
Was it hard to persuade people to rent rather than buy?

Less than I'd feared. Our first customers were students going to weddings and parties, and for them it was obvious: why spend two hundred pounds on a dress you'll wear once? The harder group has been people over forty, who tend to feel that renting clothes means you can't afford to buy them. That attitude is changing, but slowly.
So, the delivery mistakes. How did you fix that?

We stopped trying to cover the whole country. We focused on just two cities, where we could use local couriers and a laundry we trusted. Growing more slowly felt like failure at the time, and investors kept asking why we weren't expanding, but it's the reason we're still here.
How do you decide which clothes to stock?
Mostly from data. We track what people search for and can't find, and then we buy that. Instinct still plays a part, but I've been wrong often enough to trust the numbers more than my own taste.
You've been quite critical of the way fashion start-ups talk about sustainability.

I have. A lot of companies, including us at the beginning, made big claims without really measuring anything. If a dress is rented ten times, but each rental involves two journeys in a van and a chemical clean, is that actually better for the planet than one person owning it? It depends. So we now publish the numbers for every item, even when they don't make us look good.
Customers have been more understanding than I expected. What they don't forgive is being misled.

We're testing something with a few universities. Students can rent formal clothes for graduation and job interviews at a reduced price. It won't make much money, but it brings in customers who'll hopefully stay with us for years. And frankly, it's the service I wish I'd had.
